sections.html: Origin: Peru. Currently offered as wild-collected fish.

Rivulus always dwell near the water surface, and R. rubrolineatus in particular is a perfect aquarium fish for the upper region of a tank. However, the tank must be covered perfectly, because Rivulus tend to change their habitat by wandering over land. When the weather is wet, the fish jump through the land vegetation in order to reach new water. This migratory instinct also breaks out from time to time in aquaria.

The fish are very undemanding regarding food and water chemistry and fit quite well in a community tank along with peaceful tetras, catfish etc.

Males and females can be easily distinguished by coloration. If the fish show stress coloration (for example when being caught), the females can be recognized by the typical dark spot on the upper end of the caudal peduncle.
Rivulus attach their eggs in fine plant material. The eggs do not need a dry period and hatch after about two weeks.

The genus Rivulus was split into several new genera as early as 1992, but this was adopted only hesitantly. Accordingly, R. rubrolineatus belongs to the genus Anablepsoides.

In contrast to many other killifish, Rivulus rubrolineatus can reach a fairly normal age for small fish, about 3 years under aquarium conditions (much shorter in the wild).

Etymology: Rivulus: Latin, means "small brook"; probably the name was given because the describer was told the fish live in brooks. rubrolineatus: Latin, means "with red lines". Anablepsoides: in allusion to the genus Anableps (four-eyed fishes), due to the water-surface-dwelling behaviour.
